title: Hamzat al-waṣl in full, silent letters, and how to read any legend
objectives: Student can start on any word beginning with ٱ and produce the correct vowel from the verb, noun or particle branch rather than from memory.
Student never pronounces a waṣl hamzah when joining.
Student can read the round zero and the oval zero and say what each does at a join and at a stop.
Student can pick up any coloured muṣḥaf or app, find its legend, and read it — rather than assuming a palette she has memorised.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.35 — Hamzat al-waṣl, silent letters, and any legend
Two errors in ninety seconds, pulling opposite ways
body: Ask her to read 110:3 joined — فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ. Most learners produce wa-istaghfirhu, with an audible bump in the middle. It is especially common with Persian, Urdu or Turkic speech habits, because the consonant cluster that results from dropping the hamzah is not one those languages permit.
The hamzah is not there when you join. Wastaghfirhu.
Now stop her and ask her to START from ٱدْخُلُوا۟ (16:32). She will almost certainly say idkhulū.
"So one of them you are pronouncing when you shouldn't, and the other you are pronouncing wrong when you should. Both are the same letter. Today it stops being a guess."
Two errors, from opposite directions, on one letter, inside ninety seconds. That is the hook, and it works because it shows her the letter has a rule rather than a habit.

2-09 gave her the working version — the article starts with a fatḥah and the hamzah drops when joining — and she has been resuming from stops with it since 2-12. Today is the full branch structure, not a first pass.

slides.heading: The two hamzahs
body: Hamzat al-qaṭʿ is written أ إ ؤ ئ ء. It is pronounced when you start on the word and pronounced when you join from the word before. Always there. أَنْعَمْتَ · إِيَّاكَ · أَحَدٌ.
Hamzat al-waṣl is written ٱ — an alif carrying a small ص, for ṣilah, connection. It is pronounced when you START on the word and dropped entirely when you JOIN. ٱلْحَمْدُ · ٱدْخُلُوا۟ · ٱبْن.
Why it exists, in one sentence: the waṣl hamzah is there to give a sākin letter something to start on. Once there is a previous word to lean on, it is not needed and it disappears.
Her own hifz supplies the cleanest cases. وَٱنْحَرْ (108:2) is wanḥar. وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ (110:3) is wastaghfirhu. وَٱلصَّيْفِ (106:2) is waṣ-ṣayf. Never wa-inḥar, never wa-istaghfirhu.
So the whole of the rule is two questions: am I starting here, or am I joining? And if I am starting, which vowel?

slides.heading: Starting on a ٱ — three branches and nothing else
slides.condition: A waṣl hamzah is pronounced when you start on the word, and dropped entirely when you join from the word before. When you start, the vowel comes from the word's category: verb, noun, or particle.
body: Verbs — أفعال. Past tense of a five- or six-letter verb: KASRAH. اِنْطَلَقَ · اِسْتَغْفَرَ. Command of a five- or six-letter verb: KASRAH. اِنْطَلِقْ · اِسْتَغْفِرْ · اِسْتَقِمْ.

Command of a THREE-letter verb: look at the third letter of its present tense. Original ḍammah → ḍammah. اُدْخُلُوا from يَدْخُلُ · اُنظُرْ from يَنظُرُ · اُعْبُدُوا from يَعْبُدُ. Fatḥah or kasrah → kasrah. اِضْرِبْ from يَضْرِبُ · اِذْهَبْ from يَذْهَبُ · اِجْعَلْ from يَجْعَلُ.
The one exception worth naming: if that ḍammah is ʿāriḍ — accidental, arising from a deleted weak letter — the start is a kasrah anyway. اِمْشُوا (38:6) · اِبْنُوا · اِقْضُوا.
Nouns — أسماء. Seven samāʿī nouns, all kasrah, and that is the entire branch.
Particles — حروف. The definite article ال always takes a FATḤAH. اَلْحَمْدُ · اَلرَّحْمَٰن · اَلنَّاس · اَلَّذِينَ. One item, no exceptions, and by far the most frequent case.
Say the arithmetic out loud: most of the time the answer is a. The branches exist for the rest.

slides.heading: The trick that IS the verb branch — say the present tense first
body: This is the only part of today's material that needs to become a reflex, so drill it rather than explaining it twice.
يَدْخُلُ. What is on the khāʾ? A ḍammah. So the command starts udkhulū.
يَذْهَبُ. What is on the hāʾ? A fatḥah. So the command starts idhhab.

Have her do the lookup OUT LOUD, slowly, six or seven times, until it goes internal. She will not do it in real time at first, and the failure mode is not ignorance of the rule — it is that the lookup takes a second and she is reading at speed.
The seven nouns need no lookup because there is nothing to derive. اِسْم · اِبْن · اِبْنَة · اِمْرُؤ · اِمْرَأَة · اِثْنَان · اِثْنَتَان. All kasrah. Memorise the list.

Classical Arabic lists ten; اِسْت, اِيْمُن and اِبْنُم do not occur in the Qurʾān, so seven is the working number. Samāʿī means "heard" — heard, not derived, and telling her that is what stops her hunting for a rule that does not exist.
عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ (3:45) is the one to show her: joined, so the hamzah is gone; started, so it is ibnu.

slides.heading: When a waṣl hamzah lands on a sākin hamzah — and the loop from 3-31
body: A small closed set. When she STARTS on a word whose waṣl hamzah is immediately followed by a sākin hamzah, the second hamzah turns into a madd letter matching the first vowel.
ٱئْتِ (10:15) is started as إِيتِ. ٱئْتُوا۟ (20:64) is started as اِيتُوا. ٱئْذَن (9:49) is started as اِيذَن. ٱؤْتُمِنَ (2:283) is started as اُوتُمِنَ.
Four words. Show her all four, have her start on each, and move on. A closed set of four does not deserve a large share of the session.

And now the loop from 3-31 closes. ءَآلْـَٰٔنَ (10:51, 10:91) · ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ (6:143) · ءَآللَّهُ (27:59) — an interrogative hamzah landing on a hamzat al-waṣl. She met the first as madd lāzim kalimī mukhaffaf; today she can see the other half of why it is spelt that way. Six counts, or tas-hīl.
One minute on that. Do not re-teach it — just let her see that the two names describe one sound.

slides.translation: So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.

audio.cue: wanḥar, one word, no bump. The wāw of وَ leans straight onto the nūn and the alif you can see is not sounded at all. Then start on ٱنْحَرْ alone: now it is inḥar, kasrah, because it is a command of a three-letter verb whose present tense يَنْحَرُ has a fatḥah. The letter appears and disappears — that is the rule doing its job.

slides.translation: Then glorify the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.

audio.cue: wastaghfirhu. Run the two words together with no bump and say them as one. This is the word the lesson opened on, and it is inside a surah she already holds — so the correction is not hypothetical, it is a repair to something she recites.

slides.heading: Silent letters — three sources of silence, each one marked
slides.condition: A letter written but not recited. In Uthmānī orthography the muṣḥaf marks each case, and the mark tells you WHEN the letter is silent.
body: One. Hamzat al-waṣl — silent whenever you join. Everything above. It is the most frequent silent letter in the Qurʾān.

Two. The small round zero ○ — aṣ-ṣifr al-mustadīr. NEVER pronounced, joining or stopping. Pure spelling. أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ (2:5) is ulāʾika, and the wāw is never sounded. فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟ (106:3) — from her own Quraysh — is fal-yaʿbudū, and the alif is never sounded.

Three. The small oval or vertical zero ٘ — aṣ-ṣifr al-mustaṭīl al-qāʾim. Silent ONLY when joining; pronounced, two counts, when stopping. سَلَٰسِلَا۟ (76:4) is salāsila joined and salāsilā stopped. ٱلظُّنُونَا۠ (33:10) is aẓ-ẓunūna joined and aẓ-ẓunūnā stopped. وَثَمُودَا۟ (53:51) the same.

أَنَا۠ — learn this one by heart. It occurs some sixty times, and once in her own hifz: وَلَآ أَنَا۠ عَابِدٌ (109:4). The final alif is written, silent when joining, two counts at a stop. A learner who reads anā in the middle of a sentence is adding a madd that is not there.

And the contrast that actually matters: a letter carrying NO mark at all is not silent. It is merged (mudgham) or hidden (mukhfā), and it is still doing acoustic work. The absence of a sukūn is itself information. Do not let "letters can be silent" become "letters I cannot hear clearly are silent".
Hidden is not silent. Say that sentence, because the over-generalisation arrives the same session.

slides.translation: Let them worship the Lord of this House.

audio.cue: فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟ — look at the alif at the end and the small round circle sitting on it. Never pronounced, joining or stopping: fal-yaʿbudū rabba. This is in a surah she completed two sessions ago, and she has almost certainly been reading it correctly by ear without knowing there was a mark telling her to.

slides.translation: Nor will I be a worshipper of what you worship.

audio.cue: أَنَا۠ with the small oval zero. Joined onward to عَابِدٌ it is ana ʿābidun — short, no madd, straight into the next word. Stop on it deliberately, for the contrast, and it becomes anā at two counts. Same letter, same mark, two behaviours, and the difference is entirely whether you keep going.

slides.heading: Four kinds of silence, all from what she already holds

pairs.note: Silent because you joined. Start on the word instead and the hamzah comes back, with a kasrah. The only conditional one of the four.
Round zero. Silent always — joining, stopping, whatever you do. Pure spelling, and there is no reading in which that alif is sounded.
Oval zero. Silent when joining, two counts when stopping. The mark does not say 'silent'; it says 'silent unless you stop', and reading it as the round one costs a madd.
Two silences in one word: the waṣl hamzah goes because you joined, and the lām goes into the ḍād. Both grey in Family B — and the palette grouping them is telling you something true.

slides.heading: Coloured muṣḥafs do not agree with each other
body: This is the course's own addition and it is the section that matters most. End goal 4 is not "know this palette". It is "knowing what each colour demands" — on whatever page is in front of her.

State the problem plainly. The Quranly app — this course's default, and the app she actually reads — colours RED for qalqalah and BLUE for madd. The printed Dar al-Maʿrifah muṣḥaf colours RED for madd.
Both are in wide use. Both are internally consistent. They directly contradict each other on the most eye-catching colour on the page.

A learner who has memorised one palette and picks up the other will misread every red letter in the book: she will bounce her madds and stretch her qalqalahs. That is not a small error and it will not announce itself.
So the skill is not memorising a palette. The skill is asking a book what its colours mean, every time you open a new one.

"You are not learning a set of colours. You are learning to ask a book what its colours mean. Every muṣḥaf you ever pick up will answer that question if you look — and the ones that won't answer it are the ones you shouldn't trust."

slides.heading: Family B — the palette THIS course uses, and why grey is today's colour
The four steps — and she should be able to say them back
body: One. FIND THE LEGEND. Muṣḥafs print it on the first or last page; apps put it in settings or behind a "?" icon. If there is no legend anywhere, the book is not usable for identifying rules and she should not guess from it.
Two. LOOK UP RED FIRST. Red is the colour the traditions disagree about, so it is the fastest test of which family she is holding. One lookup and she knows.

Three. CHECK A WORD SHE ALREADY KNOWS. Open al-Fātiḥah and look at ٱلضَّآلِّينَ. If it is coloured and the legend says that colour is madd, she is in a madd-coloured palette. Cross-check against a qalqalah letter — the dāl of أَحَدٌ — and the two answers together confirm it.
Four. READ THE WHOLE LEGEND BEFORE YOU READ THE PAGE. Two minutes, once per book, and never again for that book.

Notice which colour today's material lives in: grey. Hamzat al-waṣl, silent letters and lām shamsiyyah all share it in Family B. The silent things have been given one colour, which is a real piece of information about how that palette thinks — and a different palette may split them.

Do this live, in the session, with whatever coloured muṣḥaf or app she actually has. If she has two, do it with both and let her find the contradiction herself. Finding it herself is worth more than being told.

slides.heading: Which vowel, and which branch
slides.instructions: I point at the word. Before you read it, say a, i or u — and then say which branch you used: article, verb, or one of the seven nouns. Answer first, read second. Twenty of these.

audio.cue: 1:2 — A. The article. Is it ٱل? Then it's an a. Always, and it is most of the words on any page.
16:32 — U. Verb branch: يَدْخُلُ has a ḍammah on the khāʾ. And note the second word is the article again, joined, so its hamzah is gone.
38:6 — I. This is the exception: يَمْشُونَ looks like a ḍammah, but it is ʿāriḍ, from a deleted weak letter. Kasrah.
3:45 — I. One of the seven nouns. Joined here, so nothing is sounded at all; started, it is ibnu.
108:2 — joined, so there is no vowel to choose. Trick question, and worth asking once.
1:7 — qaṭʿ, not waṣl. Always pronounced, joining or starting. Look at the head of the alif: no ص.

slides.heading: Present tense first
slides.instructions: Ten three-letter commands. For each one: say the present tense out loud, point at its third letter, name the vowel on it, and only then start the command. Out loud every time — the whole point is to make the lookup fast enough to survive real reading.

audio.cue: يَدْخُلُ — ḍammah on the khāʾ. So: udkhul.
يَذْهَبُ — fatḥah on the hāʾ. So: idhhab.
يَنظُرُ — ḍammah on the ẓāʾ. So: unẓur.
يَضْرِبُ — kasrah on the rāʾ. So: iḍrib.
يَعْبُدُ — ḍammah on the bāʾ. So: uʿbud.
يَجْعَلُ — fatḥah on the ʿayn. So: ijʿal.

slides.heading: Join it, start it
slides.instructions: Each word twice: once joined from the word before it, once started on. The hamzah appears and disappears. Say what happened each time.

audio.cue: 108:2. Joined: wanḥar, no bump. Started: inḥar, kasrah — يَنْحَرُ has a fatḥah.
110:3. Joined: wastaghfirhu. Started: istaghfirhu — command of a six-letter verb, so kasrah.
106:2. Joined: waṣ-ṣayf. Started: aṣ-ṣayf — the article, so a fatḥah. And the lām is shamsiyyah, so it is silent both ways.
110:1. Joined: wal-fatḥ. Started: al-fatḥ. Article again — and stopping here gives you the qalqalah on the ḥāʾ as a bonus.

slides.heading: Zeros, and the legend live
slides.instructions: For each marked letter say NEVER or ONLY AT A STOP, then read the word both ways where it applies. Then close the book and open your coloured muṣḥaf or app: find the legend, read it aloud to me, and tell me what red is in THIS book.

audio.cue: 2:5 — round zero. NEVER. Look at the little circle: that is a zero, there is no wāw, ulāʾika.
106:3 — round zero, in her own hifz. NEVER. Joined or stopped, that alif is not sounded.
109:4 — oval zero. ONLY AT A STOP. Joined: ana, short. Are you stopping on it? No? Then it is ana, straight into the next word.
76:4 — ONLY AT A STOP. Read it both ways back to back and hear the two counts appear.
33:10 — ONLY AT A STOP, and it is an āyah end, so in practice you will nearly always be stopping.
1:7 — the legend check word. Is it coloured in your book? What does the legend say that colour is? Now cross-check the dāl of أَحَدٌ, and you know which family you are holding.

mistakes.wrong: The waṣl hamzah pronounced when joining — wa-istaghfirhu, wa-inḥar.
mistakes.why: The alif is visible and she is reading it. Her first language may not permit the consonant cluster that results from dropping it, which makes the correct form physically awkward and not just unfamiliar.
mistakes.fix: Run the two words together with no bump. wastaghfirhu. Say it as one word.

mistakes.wrong: ٱلْحَمْدُ started with a kasrah — il-ḥamdu.
mistakes.why: Kasrah is the default across most branches, and the article is the exception that also happens to be the most common case on any page.
mistakes.fix: Is it ٱل? Then it's an a. Always.

mistakes.why: She has not run the present-tense lookup — not because she does not know it, but because the lookup takes a second and she is reading in real time.
mistakes.fix: يَدْخُلُ. What's on the khāʾ? A ḍammah. So: udkhulū.

mistakes.why: It is a letter, it is written, and nothing in her reading experience so far says a written letter can be pure decoration.
mistakes.fix: Look at the little circle. That's a zero. There is no wāw. ulāʾika.

mistakes.wrong: anā read in the middle of a sentence.
mistakes.why: anā is the form she knows from spoken Arabic and it is also the correct stop form, so she is right half the time and never gets corrected.
mistakes.fix: Are you stopping on it? No. Then it's ana, short, straight into the next word.

mistakes.wrong: An unmarked merged or hidden letter treated as silent.
mistakes.why: Over-generalisation from today: 'letters can be silent' becomes 'letters I can't hear clearly are silent'. It arrives within the same session.
mistakes.fix: Is there a zero over it? No? Then it's doing work. Hidden is not silent.

mistakes.wrong: Naming a colour from memory instead of from the legend.
mistakes.why: She has read one app for months and the palette has stopped feeling like a fact about the app and started feeling like a fact about tajweed.
mistakes.fix: Don't tell me what red means. Show me where the book says what red means.

slides.heading: The whole lesson in six items

audio.cue: Joined, so the hamzah is gone entirely. No bump. One word.
Started, so the hamzah is back — and يَدْخُلُ decides the vowel is a ḍammah.
The article. Fatḥah, no exceptions, and most of the time this is the answer.
Round zero. Never sounded, whatever you do.
Oval zero. Silent joining, two counts stopping. The mark says 'silent unless you stop'.
The legend check. Whatever colour this is in your book, go and read what your book says it means before you trust it.

slides.heading: Homework
tasks: Hifz: al-Fīl 105:3–5 to 20–40 repetitions daily. This is the LAST new Sabaq in the course — after today she holds al-Fātiḥah and all ten of 105–114, eleven items, complete. Mark it out loud, write the date, and let her have the moment. From tomorrow: al-Fīl whole, then al-Fātiḥah followed by 114 down to 105 in one sitting, once, to see the whole set in one piece before the capstone. Hold her to أَبَابِيلَ · سِجِّيلٍ · مَّأْكُولٍۭ — three āyah ends in a row, three madd ʿāriḍ, all at her one chosen number; بِحِجَارَةٍ read as a t because she joins straight on; and a planned breath across 105:3 → 105:4 → 105:5, which is one continuous sentence.
Find twenty ٱ words on any page. Write a, i or u beside each BEFORE you read them. Bring the page — I will mark the written answers, not the reading.
Write the seven samāʿī nouns on your card. Seven, all kasrah, and there is nothing to derive.

Read the legend of every coloured muṣḥaf or app you own. Write down, for each one, what RED means in it. If you own only one, find a second online and do it with both. This is the two-minute habit that is the whole of end goal 4.

Read Sūrat al-Kawthar and Sūrat an-Naṣr aloud and make وَٱنْحَرْ and وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ completely smooth — no bump, no glottal stop. Those two words are the whole of today's first rule, inside surahs you already hold.

drills.title: Which vowel, and which branch
drills.instructions: Answer a, i or u and name the branch BEFORE reading. Twenty a day, from any page.

audio.cue: A — article.
U — verb, يَدْخُلُ.
I — the ʿāriḍ-ḍammah exception.
I — one of the seven nouns.
Qaṭʿ. Not today's rule at all — always pronounced.

drills.title: Present tense first
drills.instructions: Say the present tense out loud, point at its third letter, name the vowel, then start the command. Ten a day until the lookup is instant.

audio.cue: يَدْخُلُ — ḍammah. udkhul.
يَذْهَبُ — fatḥah. idhhab.
يَنظُرُ — ḍammah. unẓur.
يَضْرِبُ — kasrah. iḍrib.
يَعْبُدُ — ḍammah. uʿbud.
يَجْعَلُ — fatḥah. ijʿal.

drills.title: Join it, start it
drills.instructions: Each word twice — joined, then started on. Say what happened to the hamzah each time.

audio.cue: wanḥar / inḥar.
wastaghfirhu / istaghfirhu.
waṣ-ṣayf / aṣ-ṣayf.
wal-fatḥ / al-fatḥ.

drills.title: Zeros
drills.instructions: NEVER or ONLY AT A STOP for each. Then read both ways where it applies.

audio.cue: NEVER — round zero.
NEVER — round zero, and it is in Quraysh.
ONLY AT A STOP — and here you are joining, so: ana.
ONLY AT A STOP — salāsila / salāsilā.

drills.title: The legend, live
drills.instructions: Open a coloured muṣḥaf or app. Find the legend. Read it aloud. Say what RED means in THIS book. Then check ٱلضَّآلِّينَ and the dāl of أَحَدٌ against what you just read. This is the drill you will use for the rest of your life.

audio.cue: The madd test word. If its colour is 'madd' in this legend, you are in a madd-coloured palette.
The qalqalah cross-check. Two answers that agree, and you know which family the book belongs to.

dailyChecklist: Al-Fīl 105:3–5 to 20–40 repetitions — the last new Sabaq — then al-Fātiḥah and 114 down to 105 in one sitting
Twenty ٱ words found on a page, with a / i / u written beside each before reading
Ten three-letter commands with the present tense said out loud first
وَٱنْحَرْ and وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ read completely smooth inside al-Kawthar and an-Naṣr
One coloured page, legend read first — and what RED means in that book written down

script: Open with the two corrections, in that order and inside ninety seconds: 110:3 joined, where she will insert a hamzah that is not there, then a cold start on ٱدْخُلُوا۟, where she will drop the one that is. Two errors pulling opposite ways on one letter is what makes it obvious that the letter has a rule.

Do not re-teach 2-09. She has had the working version for two units and has been resuming from stops with it since 2-12. Say that out loud — today is the full branch structure, and framing it as completion rather than as new material changes how she receives a slide that otherwise looks like a table of exceptions.

Teach the verb branch as a lookup, not as a table: say the present tense, point at the third letter, read the vowel. Make her do it out loud six or seven times. The failure in real reading is never ignorance of the rule — it is that the lookup takes a second and she is reading at speed.

Give the arithmetic on the branches: most ٱ words on any page are the article, and the article is one item with no exceptions. The branches exist for the remainder. That reframing is worth more than another example.
The four sākin-hamzah words are a closed set of four. Show all four, have her start on each, move on. Do not let a small closed set take a large share of the session.
Close the ءَآلْـَٰٔنَ loop in one minute. She met it at 3-31 as madd lāzim kalimī mukhaffaf; today she sees the other half of why it is spelt that way. Two names, one sound. Do not re-teach it.

On silent letters, teach the mark rather than the word. The round zero says never; the oval zero says silent unless you stop. Both of them occur inside her own hifz — فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟ in Quraysh and أَنَا۠ in al-Kāfirūn — so use those, not the textbook examples, and let her find that she has been reading one of them correctly by ear for weeks.

Then guard the over-generalisation immediately, because it arrives in the same session: a letter with no mark is not silent, it is merged or hidden and still doing acoustic work. Hidden is not silent. Say the sentence and make her say it back.

Section 6 is the one that matters most and it is the course's own addition. Do it live, with the actual app or muṣḥaf she owns. If she owns two, do it with both and let her find the contradiction herself — being told that palettes disagree is worth far less than watching red change meaning between two books on her own table.

The failure mode the whole section exists to prevent is naming a colour from memory. If she does it, stop her mid-sentence: show me where the book says that. It is better caught today than at the capstone.

This is the last new Sabaq in the course. When she finishes it, mark the moment properly — say it out loud, write the date. She now holds eleven items complete, and the next session asks for all of them unaided.

listenFor.item: Silence where the page says silence — the waṣl hamzah gone entirely when she joins.
listenFor.commonMistake: wa-istaghfirhu, wa-inḥar — an audible bump in the middle of the phrase.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The alif is visible and she is reading it. Her first language may not permit the consonant cluster that results from dropping it, so the correct form is physically awkward and not merely unfamiliar.
listenFor.correctionCue: Run the two words together with no bump. wastaghfirhu. Say it as one word.

listenFor.item: A clean, correctly-vowelled start whenever she resumes on a ٱ word.
listenFor.commonMistake: il-ḥamdu for the article, or idkhulū for a command whose present tense carries a ḍammah.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Kasrah is the default across most branches, so the article — the most frequent case of all — is also the exception. And the present-tense lookup takes a second she does not have while reading at pace.
listenFor.correctionCue: Is it ٱل? Then it's an a. And for the verb: يَدْخُلُ, what's on the khāʾ? A ḍammah. So udkhulū.

listenFor.item: The round zero never sounded, joining or stopping.
listenFor.commonMistake: The wāw of أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ pronounced, or the final alif of فَلْيَعْبُدُوا۟ given a length.
listenFor.whyItHappens: It is a letter, it is written, and nothing in her reading experience so far says a written letter can be pure decoration.
listenFor.correctionCue: Look at the little circle. That's a zero. There is no wāw. ulāʾika.

listenFor.item: The oval zero silent when she joins and two counts when she stops — the difference tracked to whether she is actually stopping.
listenFor.commonMistake: anā read in the middle of a sentence.
listenFor.whyItHappens: anā is the form she knows from spoken Arabic and it is also the correct stop form, so she is right half the time and has never been corrected on the other half.
listenFor.correctionCue: Are you stopping on it? No. Then it's ana, short, straight into the next word.

listenFor.item: Unmarked merged and hidden letters still doing their acoustic work — not swept into today's category.
listenFor.commonMistake: Treating a mudgham or mukhfā letter as if it were silent.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Over-generalisation from this lesson: 'letters can be silent' becomes 'letters I can't hear clearly are silent'. It arrives within the same session, usually within twenty minutes.
listenFor.correctionCue: Is there a zero over it? No? Then it's doing work. Hidden is not silent.

listenFor.item: A colour named from the legend in front of her, not from memory.
listenFor.commonMistake: "Red is qalqalah" said about a book she has not checked.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has read one app for months and the palette has stopped feeling like a fact about the app and started feeling like a fact about tajweed. The Quranly app says red is qalqalah; the printed Dar al-Maʿrifah muṣḥaf says red is madd; both are in wide use.
listenFor.correctionCue: Don't tell me what red means. Show me where the book says what red means.

teacherNotes.homework: Daily: al-Fīl 105:3–5 to 20–40 repetitions — the last new Sabaq in the course — with the Manzil rotation and Sabqi first and ten extra after any caught error, then from tomorrow al-Fīl whole and al-Fātiḥah followed by 114 down to 105 in one sitting; twenty ٱ words found on a page with a / i / u written beside each before reading, the page brought in for the written answers to be marked rather than the reading; ten three-letter commands run with the present tense said out loud first. Written: the seven samāʿī nouns on her card; and for every coloured muṣḥaf or app she owns, a written note of what RED means in it — a second one found online if she owns only one. Once in the week: al-Kawthar and an-Naṣr read aloud with وَٱنْحَرْ and وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ completely smooth, no bump, no glottal stop.
